title: Living there
hook: "abodes": a place to live all day, not only on the cushion

segments.voice: Yesterday: the right room. Kindness, compassion, gladness or equanimity, matched to whoever walks in. Did you open the right door for someone? Day two hundred forty-four.

There's a difference between visiting a place and living there. You can visit a friend's cabin for a weekend and feel wonderful. But you don't know the cabin until you've been there on a rainy Tuesday, doing the dishes, in a bad mood. It's easy to treat kindness like a weekend cabin: somewhere to visit during a quiet sit, before driving back to real life. The name the Buddha gave these four qualities says something else. Today: living there.
screen: `VISITING ISN'T LIVING.` → `A WEEKEND CABIN.` → `WHAT THE NAME SAYS.`

segments.voice: Twelve days ago we took the name brahmavihara apart: brahma, the sublime, and vihara, a dwelling, the same word used for a monastery, where monks actually live. Today, take that second half at its word. The name is not four exercises. It's four homes. The Metta Sutta, a short discourse on kindness that Theravada monks and lay people chant, makes the point directly. After describing a mind of kindness toward all beings, it says to keep this mindfulness whether standing, walking, sitting or lying down, for as long as you're awake. And it calls that way of being a sublime abiding, here and now. Standing, walking, sitting, lying down: that's the whole day. The bus stop, the grocery aisle, the moment before sleep. The cushion is where you learn the way home. It isn't the only place the home exists. There's a practical side to this, too. A house you live in gets small repairs all the time. You notice the drip and fix it. Living in kindness works the same way. Nobody stays there perfectly. You notice you've wandered into irritation, and you come back, again and again, the way you come back to your own front door at the end of the day. In this picture, the aim isn't a special feeling during meditation. It's that, little by little, these four become the ordinary weather of a life.
screen: `VIHARA: A DWELLING.` · `STANDING, WALKING, SITTING, LYING DOWN.` · `THE CUSHION TEACHES THE WAY HOME.` · `SMALL REPAIRS, ALL DAY.` · then, large: `LIVE THERE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Picture your day ahead as four checkpoints: morning, midday, afternoon, evening. At each one, you'll pause for a single breath and ask, where am I living right now? Kindness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, or somewhere else? Rehearse the first one now. One breath. Where am I? No judging the answer. Just notice it, and turn toward home. The bell holds the time.
Living there. Vihara means a dwelling: the four immeasurables are homes to live in all day, not places to visit.
Your line: live there. Check in four times today, one breath each: where am I living? Then walk back home. Day two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: The Metta Sutta is chanted in Theravada monasteries and homes, and teachers encourage bringing kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity into ordinary activity, walking, working and talking, not only into formal sitting.

pairs: where you learn the way home

the Metta Sutta says to keep them standing, walking, sitting or lying down, while awake.
vihara is the same word used for a monastery
it means a dwelling, the place where you live.
everyone wanders; the practice is noticing and coming back, like small repairs in a house.

fork.setup: you felt deeply kind on the cushion this morning. an hour later you're snapping at a slow driver. what does the Metta Sutta's teaching suggest?
options: notice where you are, and come back home, right there in the car.
save kindness for the next sit.
fork.reveal: the sutta asks for kindness standing, walking, sitting, lying down: the car is part of the house.

original.note: Pali brahmavihāra: a sublime dwelling, a place to live, not just visit.

trapdoor: what you thought: brahmavihara is a fancy word for a meditation technique.
what it means: a sublime dwelling, a home you live in all day.

what a scholar hears: vihāra, from vi + harati, can mean a way of abiding, of spending one's time, and a monastic dwelling; the Metta Sutta calls this kindness a brahmavihāra, a sublime abiding, here and now.

notes: The Metta Sutta is paraphrased; confirm the 'standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as awake' line and 'sublime abiding here' are fairly rendered.
Etymology of vihāra (vi + √hṛ) and its two senses: confirm.
Day 232 introduced the brahmaviharas as 'four rooms to live in'; this day builds on it without re-teaching the list.
